title: Basic Exception Handling: Divide by Zero
description: This problem introduces basic **exception handling** using `try`, `throw`, and `catch` blocks. Exceptions are a mechanism to deal with runtime errors gracefully, separating error-handling logic from normal logic.
constraints: You must use `std::cin` for two integer inputs. You must `throw` an `std::runtime_error` if `denominator` is 0. You must use a `try-catch` block to handle the exception. Print the error message as shown.
sampleOutput:
Enter numerator: 10
Enter denominator: 0
Error: Division by zero is not allowed.
explanation: The output shows the user prompts, their inputs, and an error message if division by zero is attempted.

title: Function Template for Max Value
description: This problem introduces **function templates**, a core feature of C++ that allows you to write generic functions that can operate on different data types without rewriting the function every time.
constraints: You must define a **function template** `get_max`. It must take two parameters of the same generic type `T` and return `T`. The function should correctly return the maximum of the two values.
sampleOutput:
Max of 10 and 20 is: 20
Max of 5.5 and 3.2 is: 5.5
Max of 'Apple' and 'Banana' is: Banana
explanation: The output shows the largest value between two arguments for different data types using a generic function.

title: Catching Multiple Standard Exceptions
description: This problem expands on exception handling by demonstrating how to `catch` different types of standard exceptions. It's common for a single `try` block to have code that can `throw` more than one exception type.
constraints: You must use `std::cin` for string and integer inputs. You must use `std::stoi()`. You must `throw std::runtime_error` for division by zero. You must use multiple `catch` blocks.
sampleOutput:
Enter number string: abc
Enter divisor: 5
Caught exception: Invalid argument for number conversion.
explanation: The output shows user prompts, their inputs, and a message describing the type of error encountered.

title: Class Template for Pair (Generic Tuple)
description: This problem introduces **class templates**, which allow you to define generic classes that can work with any data type. This is incredibly useful for creating reusable data structures.
constraints: You must define a **class template** named `Pair` templated on two types (`T1`, `T2`). It must have public member variables `first` and `second`. It must have a constructor to initialize both members.
explanation: The output displays pairs of different types, showing how the class template can hold and display values of any type.

title: Custom Exception Class: InvalidInputException
description: Beyond standard exceptions, C++ allows you to define **custom exception classes** for more specific error conditions. This improves clarity and makes error handling more precise.
constraints: You must define a custom class `InvalidInputException` inheriting from `std::runtime_error`. Its constructor must take a `const char*` message. You must `throw` this custom exception on invalid input and catch it.
sampleOutput:
Enter a positive integer: -5
Caught exception: Input must be a positive integer.
explanation: The output shows the user's input and a message if the custom exception is thrown for invalid input.

title: Class Template for a Generic Stack
description: This problem reinforces **class templates** by having you implement a basic generic data structure: a `Stack`. A stack is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) data structure.
constraints: You must define a **class template** `Stack<T>`. It must use `std::vector<T>` internally. Implement `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `is_empty` methods. `pop` and `peek` must `throw std::out_of_range` if the stack is empty.
sampleOutput:
Integer Stack:
Pushing 10, 20, 30
Top element: 30
Popped: 30
Top element: 20
Stack empty? false
Popped: 20
Popped: 10
Stack empty? true
Attempting to pop from empty stack...
Caught exception: Stack is empty.
explanation: The output demonstrates stack operations for different types and shows messages when attempting invalid operations.

title: Template Function with Constraints (C++20 Concepts)
description: This problem introduces **C++20 Concepts** (or equivalent template metaprogramming for older C++ versions), which allow you to specify constraints on template parameters. This ensures templates only work for appropriate types.
constraints: You must define a function template `print_and_add_one<T>`. For C++20, use `requires` clause to constrain `T` to types supporting `operator<<` and `++T`. For older C++, explain how you would check constraints. Demonstrate with int and double.
sampleOutput:
Processing integer:
Value: 5, Incremented value: 6
Processing double:
Value: 3.14, Incremented value: 4.14
explanation: The output shows how a generic function can process different types and display incremented values.

title: Resource Management with RAII (File Wrapper)
description: This problem combines exception handling with the **Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII)** principle. RAII is a C++ idiom where resource management (like file opening/closing) is tied to object lifetime.
constraints: You must define a class `FileHandler`. Its constructor must open a file and throw `std::runtime_error` on failure. Its destructor must close the file. It must have a `write_line` method.
sampleOutput:
Attempting to write to 'my_log.txt'...
Writing line 1.
Writing line 2.
File operations successful. File closed automatically.
explanation: The output illustrates file operations and shows that resources are managed automatically, even if exceptions occur.

title: Generic Data Processor with Policy Template
description: This problem introduces a more advanced use of **templates: the Policy-based Design pattern**. This pattern allows a class template to customize its behavior by taking another class as a template parameter.
constraints: You must define two policy classes: `UpperCasePolicy` and `LowerCasePolicy`. Each policy must have a `static std::string process(const std::string&)` method. You must define a `DataProcessor<Policy>` class template that applies the given policy.
sampleOutput:
Original string: Hello World
Processed by UpperCasePolicy: HELLO WORLD
Processed by LowerCasePolicy: hello world
explanation: The output shows how applying different policy classes changes the processing of the same input string.

title: Function Template for Generic Sorting (Bubble Sort)
description: Implementing a generic sorting algorithm using a function template is a classic way to demonstrate template power. This problem focuses on applying the **Bubble Sort algorithm** to a vector of any type.
constraints: You must define a function template `bubble_sort` taking `std::vector<T>&`. You must implement the Bubble Sort algorithm. The sorting must be in ascending order. In `main`, use it for int and double.
sampleOutput:
Original Integers: 5 2 8 1 9
Sorted Integers: 1 2 5 8 9

Original Doubles: 3.1 1.5 4.2 2.7 0.9
Sorted Doubles: 0.9 1.5 2.7 3.1 4.2
explanation: The output shows original and sorted lists for different types, demonstrating generic sorting.

title: Exception Specification with `noexcept` (C++11 and later)
description: This problem explores `noexcept` (C++11 and later), a modern C++ keyword used to indicate that a function will not throw any exceptions. This provides important optimization hints to the compiler.
constraints: You must define `void may_throw_func(int)` that throws `std::runtime_error` if `val == 0`. You must define `void noexcept_func(int) noexcept` that calls `may_throw_func`. `noexcept_func` must not catch exceptions.
sampleOutput:
Calling noexcept_func with 5:
Inside may_throw_func
Value is not zero.
Normal execution continued after non-throwing call.

Calling noexcept_func with 0 (this should terminate the program)...
Inside may_throw_func
explanation: The output shows the function calls and their outcomes, highlighting the effect of the noexcept specification.

title: Generic Data Analytics Tool with Error Reporting
description: You are building a generic data analytics tool that can perform various operations (e.g., sum, average, min, max) on different types of numeric data (`int`, `double`). This tool must report errors for invalid operations using custom exceptions.
constraints: You must define a custom exception `DataAnalyticsException` inheriting from `std::runtime_error`. You must define a **class template** `AnalyticsProcessor<T>`. It must use `std::vector<T>` and provide sum, average, and max methods. Throw on empty data.
sampleOutput:
Integer Data Analysis:
Sum: 35
Average: 7.00
Max: 10

Double Data Analysis:
Sum: 22.20
Average: 5.55
Max: 8.80

Attempting to analyze empty data set:
Caught data analytics exception: Data set is empty
explanation: The output shows the result of analytics operations for different data types and demonstrates error handling for missing data.
